title: Stages of Development and the Priority of Virtue
english: Those performing priestly services seem to profane the Sabbath. Or perhaps, according to the assumption of those saying, 'your disciples are doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath' (Matt 12:2), he shows by this word that the priestly things are not transgressions, for they are not considered so, but are without fault; for he who does these things does not break the Sabbath.

One finds rest from the world, its activity, and its desire, for 'Come to me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest' (Matt 11:28). There is a higher lifting up, which the divine ones call the Sabbath-rest to be spoken of. Just as someone walking on earth has his citizenship in heaven, so someone being in the world yet doing his work from above, he sabbathizes. The Sabbath did not simply renounce work, but service. And the priestly exaltation, being supra-cosmic, makes [one] free.

These are not works of God as works of service, nor are they things God works, but things He commands to be worked by those who obey Him. And he shall receive not something else instead of the corruptible, but the corruptible itself changing into incorruption, and the very psychic becoming spiritual. See then what he says: the other of the body is incorporeal. If anyone says that what we shall receive is a different body, he does not know what is said; for he has arranged 'body' regarding both: 'a corruptible body is sown, an incorruptible body is raised; a weak and dishonorable body is sown, a strong and glorious body is raised; a psychic body is sown, a spiritual body is raised' (1 Cor 15:42-44). In a certain way, then, it is both something different and the very thing being raised is [different from] the fallen one. If he says that if there is a psychic body, there is also a spiritual body, he says in his thought that...

There is no difference, and he says: 'not first the spiritual but the psychic, then the spiritual'. The first and the second seem to be two, but I say two as if I say the man is first an infant, then a child, and not first a child but an infant, and I do not say two hypostases of a human, I do not say two men but one; but two ages. Just as the ages do not make the one growing up to maturity a different substance, but by way of manner and mind and change or transition occurs, so also from the child a man is made and the man is not a different man from the child, but the same man.

Someone truly and bodily becomes in heaven and sabbathizes, no longer walking upon the earth and having his citizenship in the heavens, but already having settled in those heavenly regions, already abiding there under the 'great high priest who has passed through the heavens' (Heb 4:14). And that he did not begin the things concerning men from wickedness, but from virtue, 'for remembrance' he says 'concerning the Sabbath'. When someone becomes in virtue, he is reminded that he once was in it.

Therefore I wish to hint at a deep word. If the beginning of men and of the soul is from this living, then wickedness is before virtue, but virtue is to be taken up. We have life with the body, we have life even without it. And that having cast off the body we become in incorporeal life, is evident everywhere. Let it be sought, whether this too was before the body. It is not manifest, but let it be sought and examined.

If, therefore, the life of the rational is from the entering-in life, then wickedness is before virtue; for we see that being filled from wickedness, the Word begins. But if, as it is the truth, virtue is before wickedness—for 'God has made man upright, but they sought out evil counsels' (Wis 1:13)—and see that the seeking of evil counsels is after the uprightness. And virtue prepares the uprightness. 'A man being in honor did not understand, he was cast down with the irrational animals' (Ps 49:20). It did not come from a beastly manner to the man, but from the human to the beastly it came. And in every way the beautiful things are always before the false things. It is necessary for skill to be before bad skill; to know something erroneously is after knowing it correctly; for how can we...

title: Instruction vs Wrathful Punishment
english: To say entirely that this is erring, unless we knew the straight path? For this reason, therefore, [it is] 'for the remembrance in the Sabbath' (Ps 94:11). And since keeping the Sabbath is to spend time in virtue and to live pleasingly to God and to serve by doing what God wills, human life began from virtue; but this does not appear in the more bodily life; for virtue is something to be taken up by those with bodies, it is something to be taught. Therefore, the one becoming in the good is remembered.

But what is the thirty-seven? It is not something one can impose on everyone. Now, someone might say this: that the thirty-seven is composed of two holy numbers; for the three is indeed praised in the Scripture. But, neglecting the tithes, it brings only one of the fruits of the holy earth; for 'one hundred, and sixty, and thirty.' And so that we may not always say the same things, it is sufficient to say everything in all things: that the number three is holy, whether it is taken in units, or in tens, or in hundreds. And the seven is also holy; for often regarding this it has been said that it is incorruptible, it is a virgin, it is without seed, it is without womb. 'Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor discipline me in your wrath' (Ps 119:125). One does not avoid being rebuked or disciplined at all, but in anger and wrath. Yet it is possible for someone to be disciplined logically and systematically, according to what is signified by the holy one praying—or rather praising and blessing—saying: 'Blessed is the man whom you will discipline, Lord, and from your law you will teach him' (Ps 119:99). He showed that this discipline happens through instruction.

And often there is also rebuke and discipline through anger and wrath, through harsh things, through bitter things. And often there is rebuke when the one in whom the error is, is shown by word to the responsible party; for this says: 'Rebuke the wise, and he will love you' (Prov 9:8). The wise man rebukes the lesser wise man, the one being led in. And again: 'But all things being rebuked are made manifest by the visible light' (Eph 5:13). And many say such things about rebuke, that rebuke is like a syllogism of contradiction. Let us say, for instance, someone is in wickedness. The one dividing the wickedness from virtue, bringing a syllogistic argument and recognizing the good, takes the bad into mind. And this rebuke is not one happening in anger.

But it is in instruction; for the knowledge of opposites is one, if we know the good, we shall have knowledge of the evil. And from the Scriptures one can take examples: the Ninevites had become in much wickedness, as if 'their cry of wickedness had ascended' (Jonah 4:11) to God calling for punishment and retribution. But God sent a proclamation of repentance. They approached the proclamation. They were instructed and reproved, not in wrath or anger. For example, the Sodomites were reproved and instructed in wrath and anger. Therefore, He does not want to be reproved in this way, not even to be reproved properly while setting aside [the alternative].

'For your arrows have struck me' (Psalm 69:4). Because of this, I avoid the reproof that is in wrath and the instruction that is in anger, since 'your arrows have struck into me' (Psalm 69:4). They gained knowledge of the punishments being brought against the uninstructed, against the unreprovable. Often, the arrows of divine instruction signify the punishments; as if Job, having become in many afflictions, says: 'The arrows of the Lord are in my body' (Job 6:4). That terrible pull, he said 'arrows of the Lord' finding itself in his body. And the paradoxical thing: providence is introduced through this word. These heavy things, such as arrows, signify to me: that unless by the judgment of God, these heavy things would have risen above me; 'for the arrows are of the Lord, whose wrath pours out my blood; when I begin to speak, they pierce me' (Psalm 7:13). And see, that the heavy thing and that evil pull, he said 'arrows of the Lord.' And again in the great Psalm 171 of Deuteronomy, God says: 'I will drink my arrows from blood, and my sword shall devour the blood of the wounded' (Deuteronomy 32:42). Often again the sword signifies punishment: 'for if,' he says, 'you will not wish nor listen, a sword shall fall upon you' (Deuteronomy 32:41). Such also is that which is said in Isaiah: 'My sword has become drunk in heaven' (Isaiah 34:6), instead of: the punishment has touched heavenly things. And if God subjected 'the angels who did not keep their own dominion' (Jude 1:6) to 'eternal chains,' the sword of God—that is, the punishing power—has become drunk, and in heaven. title: The Piercing Arrows and the Hand of God
english: The sword is intoxicated in heaven, regarding the promised possession of a heavenly citizenship. Such is the saying: 'Sons of the kingdom, you shall be cast into the outer darkness' (Matt 13:41-42); for they are not [the ones] who exist. But it is also taken as praiseworthy: 'Your arrows, having been shot, O Mighty One, shall cause peoples under you to fall' (Ps 126:4). Your words, having been shot, are directed toward passion and love; for you are powerful and you powerfully send out your words, and you direct those who are being cast [by them] toward love. Likewise, the soul undergoing this—that is, the Church—says: 'Pierced by love am I' (Song 8:6). Thus, the arrows are both praiseworthy and piercing. Since these were named with wrath and fury, they are not directed toward passion and love, but are producing a sensation, of which there is some evil.

And you have placed your hand upon me. Often again, the punishing power is signified by the name of the hand of God; as if saying to Pharaoh: 'Now, having sent the hand, I will strike you' (Ex 7:17). And: 'Behold, the hand of the Lord shall fall upon your livestock in the fields' (Ex 9:3); for those livestock were struck down with destruction. And again it is said: 'Your hand has destroyed the nations' (Ps 18:47). When the active, creative, and covering hand of God is named, it is called 'the right hand.' For this indeed leads toward salvation. He who has experienced being guided by it says: 'You have grasped the hand of my right hand' (Ps 63:8), the practical power of the good.

And there is no healing for my flesh from the presence of your wrath. The name 'flesh' signifies different things according to the Scripture, being homonymous. It is sometimes said that 'flesh' signifies our sensory choice; for when it is said: 'I will break their stony heart from them and put a fleshy one in' (Ezek 36:26), 'stony heart' means the flinty intellect having been deprived of all sensation. In its place, a fleshy one is placed, sensory and yielding to the laws of God. Thus, the yielding and the sensory are often called flesh. And 'flesh' is also said to be being cut off from the spirit. 'Spirit' means the intention, while 'flesh' means that which is being cut off from the intention.
